note: An archive whose root document declares a larger payload than it holds. Section 7 bounds an entry's payload by the following local header rather than by the size a header declares, so a conforming reader returns the document and reports nothing: the declared size is not a fact a reader may trust and not a cause for refusal. Measured here: `doc.vnx` declares 146 bytes in both its local header and its central directory entry, holds 139, and carries a CRC computed over the 139 that are there - so the over-declaration is 7 bytes and the checksum is correct for the real payload. Two things about its POSITION are load-bearing rather than incidental. It is the SECOND of three entries, so its local header is not at offset 0 and a reader that loses an offset and defaults to zero does not still land on it - the mistake that made an earlier ZIP64 fixture pass with its extra-field parser disabled. And a third entry follows it, so the bound on its payload comes from a FOLLOWING LOCAL HEADER rather than from the central directory or the end of the file, which is the more interesting of the two paths and the one a reader is likelier to get wrong. Moving `doc.vnx` to first or last removes one of those properties each, and nothing goes red. THIS CASE IS PASSED TRIVIALLY BY A READER THAT NEVER COMPARES SIZES, and that is the rule rather than a weakness: section 7 forbids refusing on the discrepancy and does not require noticing it. What the case excludes is the reader that TRUSTS the declared size, which is the common implementation and the one every stock library takes. Measured: Go's archive/zip refuses this entry with `zip: checksum error`, because it reads the declared count and checksums what it read; Python's zipfile refuses it as `Overlapped entries`. So a VNX reader built on either, without care, fails this case - which is the whole reason it exists. Hand-built, because section 7.1 forbids a conforming writer to produce it: no round-trip through any writer in this repository can reach this archive, and that is why nothing caught the defect until a fixture existed. It is the corpus's only witness for section 7's size rule. Attachments are listed in archive order because section 7 does not order a reader's attachment list; a reader sorting them is equally conforming, and a runner comparing this field must not depend on the order.
